n: A prophecy titled “the desert of the sea,” a cryptic name for Babylon, which lay in flat marshland near the Persian Gulf. Disaster sweeps in like desert whirlwinds.

f.g: Southern Mesopotamia — Babylon’s region, once called “the Sealand.”
Fierce storms from the Negev desert.

n: Isaiah receives a harsh vision: betrayers betray and destroyers destroy. Elam and Media are called to attack. Media and Persia (whose homeland included Elam) conquered Babylon in 539 BC, ending the groaning it had caused.

f.g: A land east of Babylon, in southwest Iran; part of the Persian empire.

n: The vision is so terrible that Isaiah feels pain like a woman in labor. He is staggered by what he hears and sees.

f.g: The midsection — the body’s core.
Doubled over in distress.

n: His heart pounds with terror. The evening he hoped would be peaceful has become a night of dread.

f.g: The twilight he longed for.

n: Isaiah pictures Babylon’s leaders feasting while danger approaches — then the alarm: “Get up, officers, oil your shields!” Daniel 5 describes Belshazzar’s feast on the night Babylon fell.

f.g: Oil leather shields to prepare for battle.

n: The Lord tells Isaiah to post a lookout who will report what he sees.
The lookout sees riders — pairs of horsemen, and riders on donkeys and camels — and watches closely.

f.g: Here a troop of riders.

n: Then he cries out like a lion: “My lord, day and night I have stood at my post!”

f.g: The Dead Sea Isaiah scroll reads “the seer” — “Then the seer cried.”
Guard post.

n: Here comes a rider with news: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen! Her idols lie shattered.” Revelation repeats this cry for the fall of spiritual Babylon.

f.g: Carved idols.

n: Isaiah addresses his own people, crushed like grain on a threshing floor: what he has heard from the Lord, he has told them. Babylon’s fall would mean freedom for exiled Judah.

f.g: My people who have been threshed — beaten down by oppression.
Grain of my threshing floor.

n: A short prophecy about Dumah, an oasis in Arabia (also meaning “silence”). Someone calls from Seir (Edom): “Watchman, how much of the night is left?” They long for the end of oppression.

f.g: An oasis in northern Arabia; the name means “silence.”
The mountain region of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

n: The watchman answers: “Morning is coming — but also night.” Relief will be brief, and more darkness follows. If you want to ask, come back and ask again.

f.w: The morning cometh, and also the night
f.g: A short relief, then more trouble.
Or “turn” — perhaps an invitation to repent.

n: A prophecy about Arabia: traveling caravans of Dedan will have to camp in the thickets instead of on open trade routes, hiding from danger.

f.g: Dedanites, an Arabian trading tribe.
Thickets or scrubland.

n: The people of Tema bring water and bread to refugees fleeing the war — a picture of hospitality in hard times.

f.g: An oasis city in northwest Arabia.
Met, came to meet.

n: These refugees are fleeing swords, drawn bows, and the horrors of war.

f.g: A bow drawn and ready to shoot.

n: Within one year, counted exactly as a hired worker counts, the glory of Kedar will end. Assyria campaigned against Arabian tribes in this period.

f.g: A powerful nomadic Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13).

n: Only a few of Kedar’s mighty archers will survive. The Lord God of Israel has spoken it.

f.g: Remainder.
